pr_title: lib: implement interface converter and use it for AbortSignal validation
pr_body:
This PR contains 2 commits. 

The first one implements interface converter as per [the spec](https://webidl.spec.whatwg.org/#js-interface).
The one after uses the implemented interface converter to properly validate `AbortSiganl`s in `AbortSignal.any`

Fixes: https://github.com/nodejs/node/issues/54962

I am marking this as https://github.com/nodejs/node/labels/semver-major since as far as I understand, this would break for any user-land implementation of `AbortSignal` (https://www.npmjs.com/package/abort-controller etc)

> I am marking this as [semver-major](https://github.com/nodejs/node/labels/semver-major)

I agree this would be a semver-major. Does it mean a CITGM is required?

> this would break for any user-land implementation of `AbortSignal`

Would it be better to remove [this change](https://github.com/nodejs/node/pull/54965/files#diff-03bd4f07a1006cb0daaddced702858751b20f5ab7681cb0719c1b1d80d6ca05cL445-R447)? This is unrelated to the issue that the PR is fixing and it can be avoided.
Is there any documentation for supporting third party abortcontrollers? If not I could see this landing as a bug fix.

There is only one benchmark test coverring `abort_controller` and it's only covering the `AbortController.abort`, which is, IMO, not affected by this PR.

@anonrig In that case, would it be better if I raise another PR to add benchmark tests to cover `AbortSignal.any` and `aborted`, which are the ones affected by this PR, before proceeding this?

To be clear - since this breaks userland I want to see how the TSC and namely people who were involved in the original discussion ( @jasnell @mcollina @ronag ) feel about this change.

I'm personally +0 (I'd like it but not at the cost of extensive breakage)
We made the same decision in undici to drop third party AbortController/AbortSignal support.

Thinking about this more userland AbortController libraries have tens of millions of weekly downloads so I'm -0.5 (not for this change but still not blocking)

> We made the same decision in undici to drop third party AbortController/AbortSignal support.

When did it happen (assuming it affects Node's `fetch`)? Was there any breakage?

I am -1 for this change.
The top 4 user-land implementations on npm have almost 60 million weekly downloads

> When did it happen (assuming it affects Node's fetch)? Was there any breakage?

v7, which is releasing soon-ish. Breakage is unimportant here - it was undocumented behavior that broke compatibility with other implementations and the spec. If we implement a spec, we need to accept its burden too. If there are/were performance concerns, those need to be fixed in node core, not handed off to user land to create crappy (not to be offensive) abortcontroller implementations to be used instead.

Would like share some of my humble opinions here.

1. **Standard is more important to pursue compared to the support of 3rd party library** - If we take a step back and look at this issue itself, it points out an inconsistency between node and other runtimes. Just because of that, it's a must fix, as the whole point of having a standard (please correct me if I'm wrong) is to allow users to confidently write code to be run any runtime without conditional check. From that sense, the original issue breaks that, and I don't see other ways to do so without brand checking.

2. **Number of downloads is not an accurate factor to consider** - This change specifically updates for the validation of `AbortSignal.any`. (let's not think about the `aborted()`, as it can be taken out of the PR.) AFAIK, the only way the userland could break is when they use a combination of `ThirdPartyAbortController` and node's `AbortSignal.any`.
    ```
    AbortSignal.any([new ThirdPartyAbortController().signal ])
    ```
    That is, even though there are 60,000,000 weekly downloads, it doesn not mean this could extensively break their users (yes, not the library itself, but their users, e.g. [some of library](https://github.com/mysticatea/abort-controller) doesn't use `AbortSignal.any`). 

    So what factor should we look at? Honestly, I don't know. I don't have other factor to look at to justify how breaky it is, but just want to point out not to too focus on the number of downloads for this PR. If the PR is overhauling the `validateAbortSignal` function, then absolutely, the number of downloads is a good indicator and CITGM will definitely tell us something.

I think the decision to make is whether or not we want to phase in brand check completely, i.e. drop support to 3rd party libs, or leaving it half-half is acceptable?
FWIW the "breakability" of some libraries can be tested with a CITGM

> I'd like it but not at the cost of extensive breakage

The cost of keeping support for 3rd party implementation is maintainers' headaches. Long-term is an untenable proposition.

> v7, which is releasing soon-ish. Breakage is unimportant here - it was undocumented behavior that broke compatibility with other implementations and the spec. If we implement a spec, we need to accept its burden too.

This is true for `AbortSignal.any` and `fetch` but none of the other many Node.js APIs that currently take AbortSignals. The breakage can be nontrivial and at the very least this would need a CITGM run given userland implementations of AbortSignal have tens of millions of weekly downloads.

If we remove a feature, we need to assess breakage and minimize it.

> If we remove a feature, we need to assess breakage and minimize it.

In addition to CITGM, is there anything else I can do to help assess the breakage? IIUC, the users we concern here are mostly the users using 3rd party `AbortSignal` library with the code running on `Node`.

To minimize the influence, would it be helpful if this goes into deprecation cycle, considering this was a feature. (not a suggestion but just having this question : ))

issue_context.title: `{aborted: false}` is treated as valid `AbortSignal` but not in other runtimes
issue_context.body:
### Version

v22.8.0

### Platform

```text
N/A
```


### Subsystem

abort controller

### What steps will reproduce the bug?

```
AbortSignal.any([ { aborted: false }])
```

### How often does it reproduce? Is there a required condition?

100%

### What is the expected behavior? Why is that the expected behavior?

Fail with TypeError

### What do you see instead?

Passed

### Additional information

This fails in other runtime like Chrome and Firefox
comments: Can you provide the exact error given by other runtimes?

In Firefox:
```
>> AbortSignal.any([ { aborted: false }])
Uncaught TypeError: AbortSignal.any: Element of argument 1 does not implement interface AbortSignal.
    <anonymous> debugger eval code:1
```

In Chrome:
```
> AbortSignal.any([ { aborted: false }])

VM176:1 Uncaught TypeError: Failed to execute 'any' on 'AbortSignal': Failed to convert value to 'AbortSignal'.
    at <anonymous>:1:13
```

This was a deliberate design choice (to not brand check) in order to have better ecosystem compatibility.

Now that we've had AbortSignal for a few years it's fine to revisit

review_comments:
Good suggestion. I will update the argument name instead of the comment. The comment is from the spec and I think it will be clearer if the argument is consistent with the spec. 

Update: Done
Shouldn't we update `validateAbortSignal` – or remove it if we no longer need it?

I tried updating it, but it breaks some tests, as it is used variously in other modules. Some modules treat `EventTarget` with `{ aborted: boolean; }` as a valid `AbortSignal`, and its test is written in that way.

This error message change is not semver-major nor minor, as there is only one place using this converter and it's not using the `context`, i.e. the error message is not even displayable in the userland.
I'd recommend replacing opts with a string argument.

I tried with that, but it might not be ideal. The `opts` in the returned converter can be used in `createSequenceConverter`, which creates a different converter based on an incoming converter. It assumes the incoming one takes `opts` as object.

TL;DR these `opts` need to be consistent across all converters.
In undici I replaced object arguments with strings for perf, but this should be left for another PR
